I'll analyze each chunk against the Chapter 5B evidence criteria. Let me work through them systematically.

**Chunk U0061 — Mexico: Debt Coverage and Disclosures (DSA Annex III)**
- Contains: Debt coverage perimeter definitions (subsector inclusion/exclusion matrix), accounting basis (cash vs non-cash), valuation methods (nominal/face/market), intra-government holdings reporting (zeros), and staff commentary on Mexico's fiscal accounts classification (state/local governments excluded; debt not consolidated across federal government and NFPS).
- Material evidence: a concrete qualification about the DSA perimeter — state and local governments excluded from coverage, debt not consolidated across federal government and NFPS, gross (not net) reporting — and the fact that staff lack data on accounts payables. This bears on credibility/transparency of fiscal reporting (5B.7) and the operational rules behind debt/fiscal metrics (5B.3).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0062 — Mexico: Public Debt Structure Indicators (Annex III Figure 3)**
- Contains: time-series shares of FX vs local currency debt, holder composition (external private/official, domestic banks, "domestic other creditors"), instrument breakdown (marketable vs nonmarketable), maturity profile (≤1yr/1–5yr/>5yr, residual maturity 9.2 years), governing-law split (domestic vs international vs multilateral), and staff commentary on FX share stability, rising domestic pension-fund holdings tied to recent pension reforms, longer-maturity share rising through 2025 under the government's debt management strategy.
- Material evidence: named debt-management policy objective (lengthening maturities through 2025), attribution to "recent pension reforms" driving domestic non-bank holdings, residual maturity figure, and explicit composition shifts with policy attribution. Bears on 5B.3 (financial/debt rules, debt management), 5B.4 (predictable regulation via debt strategy), 5B.7 (published structure data).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0063 — Mexico: Baseline Scenario (Annex III Figure 4)**
- Contains: full baseline debt dynamics table 2021–2031 (public-debt-to-GDP path 56.2→57.7→58.2→58.6→58.9→59.3→58.9→58.4→57.6→56.8), contributions of primary deficit, automatic debt dynamics, r–g differential, real interest and growth rates, gross financing needs (~11–12% of GDP), and staff commentary attributing the 2023 debt-ratio increase to slowing global/Mexican GDP growth despite the primary deficit contribution; the medium-term commentary states Mexico's r–g dynamics will not lower the debt ratio and that the primary budget surplus is expected to offset unfavorable automatic debt dynamics, with explicit claim that Mexico has a "strong track record in maintaining a prudent fiscal policy stance."
- Material evidence: explicit fiscal-stance attribution ("strong track record in maintaining a prudent fiscal policy stance"), measured medium-term debt trajectory with r–g verdict, primary-surplus offset claim, and quantified policy-relevant projections for 2022–2027. Bears on 5B.3 (fiscal/monetary/financial rules), 5B.6 (budget execution outcomes), 5B.9 (shock response context), 5B.10 (durable trajectory vs inherited).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0064 — Mexico: Realism of Baseline Assumptions (Annex III Figure 5)**
- Contains: forecast track-record percentile placement for public-debt-to-GDP, primary deficit, r–g, exchange-rate depreciation, SFA; bond issuance maturity profile (5+ yr / 1–5 yr / <1 yr term) with spreads vs 10-yr US Treasuries and Laubach-rule implied spread; 3-year debt reduction above 75th percentile (5.9 ppt of GDP, percentile rank 71); 3-year CAPB adjustment percentile rank 54.1; staff commentary concluding track record is "generally within bounds for optimism," debt-creating flows compositionally similar between past/next 5 years, lengthening of bond maturities marks a break with the past 5 years and "reflects debt management objectives," and that three-year debt/CAPB adjustments are above the comparator median but well below Mexico's past maximum.
- Material evidence: quantified realism check (percentile ranks 71 and 54.1, 5.9 ppt 3-year debt reduction), attribution of maturity lengthening to "debt management objectives," and a contrary qualification (SFA projections outside bounds; pandemic-period composition bias). Bears on 5B.3 (debt-management credibility), 5B.7 (audit/independent evaluation evidence), 5B.9 (shock/prudent stance), 5B.10 (trajectory durability).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0065 — Mexico: Medium-Term Risk Analysis (Annex III Figure 6)**
- Contains: debt fanchart width 32.0, probability of debt not stabilizing 52.2 pct, terminal debt level × institutions index 35.9; GFN financeability indexes (average GFN 11.6; bank claims on government 26.9 pct of bank assets; change in claims under stress 12.1 pct); final MTI = 0.3, "Moderate"; false-alarm 21.6 pct, missed-crisis 27.3 pct; staff commentary concluding moderate risk of sovereign stress, the banking system should be able to absorb increased GFN under stress, and institutional investors (pension funds) could likely absorb additional financing needs.
- Material evidence: quantified moderate-risk verdict, banking/pension absorption finding, missed-crisis probability 27.3 pct. Bears on 5B.3 (financial stability), 5B.7 (independent risk evaluation), 5B.9 (shock-response capacity).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0066 — Mexico: External Debt Sustainability narrative (Section B)**
- Contains: gross external debt projected at ~32% of GDP end-2022 (below pre-pandemic 37%); decline attributed to rebound and continued excess capacity with strong remittance inflows producing small current-account deficits; downside risks enumerated (growth underperformance, higher risk premia, currency depreciation), with mitigation factors — favorable maturity (>90% residual maturity > 1 year), currency composition (~30% of external public debt peso-denominated), prudent debt management; quantified shock: 30% real effective peso depreciation → external debt to ~46% of GDP; private sector FX risk "well-covered by natural and financial hedges"; banking sector assessed resilient.
- Material evidence: explicit attribution to "prudent debt management by the government," quantified shock resilience, and a measured finding that remittances are at "levels well above recent historical averages." Bears on 5B.3 (debt/macro rules), 5B.8 (cross-border incidence via remittance flows), 5B.9 (shock-response framework), 5B.10 (durable trajectory).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0067 — Mexico: External Debt Sustainability Bound Tests (Annex III Figure 7)**
- Contains: bound-test charts for interest-rate shock, growth shock, non-interest current-account shock, combined shock (¼ SD on real interest rate, growth, current account), and one-time 30% real depreciation shock; baseline path 33% of GDP in 2023 across scenarios; combined-shock endpoint 38; real-depreciation shock endpoint 47; footnoted methodology (permanent ½ SD shocks; ten-year historical averages).
- Material evidence: quantified shock scenarios with explicit magnitudes (30% real depreciation → 47%; combined ¼ SD shock → 38%) and methodology footnotes that characterize the analytical procedure. Bears on 5B.3 (macro/financial rule resilience), 5B.9 (shock-response modeling), 5B.7 (transparent publication of stress tests).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0068 — Mexico: External Debt Sustainability Framework table (Annex III Table 1)**
- Contains: full external-debt trajectory 2017–2027, identified debt-creating flows decomposition (current account excluding interest, non-debt creating capital inflows, automatic debt dynamics with nominal interest, real GDP growth, price/FX contributions), external debt-to-exports ratio, gross external financing needs in USD billions and % of GDP, historical-average scenario endpoints (32.0 → 39.6), historical standard deviations and 10-year averages for real GDP growth, USD GDP deflator, nominal external interest rate, export/import growth, current-account balance, non-debt inflows; debt-stabilizing non-interest current account = -2.0.
- Material evidence: extensive measured baseline outcomes and assumptions that ground the durability assessment (e.g., debt-stabilizing non-interest CA -2.0%, nominal external interest rate path, USD deflator assumptions). Bears on 5B.3 (macro/financial framework), 5B.6 (outcome measurement), 5B.9 (shock baselines), 5B.10 (trajectory).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0069 — Mexico: Subcontracting Law, Employment, and GDP Measurement (Annex IV, paras 1–3 + manufacturing/retail charts)**
- Contains: April 2021 enactment of legislation restricting workforce subcontracting, with stated aims of preventing labor-law violations and tax evasion; the law bans service firms from providing employees supervised by a third party (specialized services and intra-group services still permitted), tightens registration/reporting, and makes non-compliance a criminal offence; compliance deadline Sept 1, 2021; historical context (subcontracted share of employment 6% in 2003 → 15% in 2018; >40% in utilities, 36% in financial services per 2019 economic census); measured outcome — subcontracted employment fell 87% in manufacturing and 70% in retail trade vs Q1 2021 by end-Q3 2021; total employment unchanged.
- Material evidence: named policy action (April 2021 subcontracting reform), compliance deadline, enforcement mechanism (criminal offence), specific measured outcomes (87%/70% subcontracting reductions, no aggregate employment change), and the distribution across sectors (utilities, financial services baseline shares). Bears on 5B.1 (legislative agenda vs rents — explicitly anti-evasion), 5B.4 (fair laws for job creation), 5B.5 (anti-evasion enforcement), 5B.8 (distributional incidence — labor-form reclassification), 5B.6 (implementation finding on outcomes).
- Decision: include.

**Chunk U0070 — Mexico: Subcontracting Law (Annex IV, paras 4 + GDP measurement chart)**
- Contains: GDP-measurement implication — value-added from workers now recorded in the sector of contract rather than employment; provisional quarterly data show real value-added decline in support services to business in 2022Q2–Q3; employment developments imply value-added should rise in directly employing sectors, but provisional data show only broadly stable growth and "no substantial change in the ratio of value added to production yet," suggesting the standard quarterly national-accounts methodology may not yet fully capture the structural change; underlying economic conditions in H2 2021 could thus have been stronger than reported, though the pandemic recovery was still relatively slower than peers.
- Material evidence: a measured distributional/output finding (value-added shift across sectors), a methodological qualification (national accounts not yet capturing structural change), and a contrary-finding note (reported slowdown may overstate weakness). Bears on 5B.7 (reliable economic information and independent evaluation; correction when evidence shows methodological gap), 5B.6 (measured budget/sectoral outcome), 5B.8 (distributional incidence across sectors).
- Decision: include.
